stem: Evaluate the definite integral of 4x^3 with respect to x from x = 1 to x = 2.

per_option_rationale.rationale: Antiderivative of 4x^3 is x^4. Applying limits: 2^4 - 1^4 = 16 - 1 = 15.
Forgetting to divide by the new exponent when integrating: antiderivative taken as 4x^4 instead of x^4. Result: 4(2^4) - 4(1^4) = 64 - 4 = 60.
Evaluating only at the upper limit and ignoring the lower limit: antiderivative = x^4, so 2^4 = 16, with the lower limit not subtracted.
Using the wrong upper limit, treating the problem as integrating from 1 to 3: 3^4 - 1^4 = 81 - 1 = 80.

explanation: Integration of a power function: integral of x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1). For 4x^3, the antiderivative is 4 * x^4/4 = x^4. Apply the limits: [x^4] from 1 to 2 = 2^4 - 1^4 = 16 - 1 = 15.

explanation_sections.punchline: When the coefficient equals the new exponent, the division cancels out cleanly, giving x^4 as the antiderivative of 4x^3.
explanation_sections.approach: Power rule for integration: raise the exponent by one and divide by the new exponent. Then subtract the antiderivative at the lower limit from the antiderivative at the upper limit.
explanation_sections.lesson: Always subtract the lower-limit value from the upper-limit value; omitting the lower limit gives a wrong answer even when the antiderivative is correct.
explanation_sections.timing: 30-40 seconds. Opt 2 (60) is the classic trap of forgetting to divide by the new exponent. Opt 3 (16) is the trap of forgetting to subtract the lower limit.
